intro.heading: The review is on Friday. What does Priya actually have?
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: Priya is the key worker for Mrs Okafor, who has dementia and lives on the first floor. Every month she sits down with the manager to review how things are going. Over the last six weeks, Mrs Okafor's daughter has sent a few photos and a short video of the church choir. Priya knows staff have been using some of it, but she could not say which items, how often, or who else has seen it. She wants to bring something specific to the review, not a general feeling.

trail.text: Mrs Okafor's daughter agrees to share photos and a video.
The manager approves the first items.
A carer plays the choir video one afternoon. It goes well.
Staff mention it at handover, but nobody writes it down.
Another carer is unsure which items have been approved.
Priya cannot say what has been played, or by whom.
The daughter asks whether anything has been used. Nobody knows.
“How does the key worker use what the family tells you?” A general answer.

trail_close: The family did their part, and the review still ran on memory. Here is how a key worker can use the tools in CareStream before the review, with the limits stated plainly.

why.heading: Why the key worker role needs something to look at
why.sub: A review is only as good as what you bring to it.

cards.title: Families know what works
cards.body: A daughter's story, a choir recording or a photo of a garden gives a key worker real material. Good person centred care examples are usually small and specific, and they come from people who know the person best.

cards.title: It supports the plan
cards.body: Under regulation 9, care must meet people's needs and reflect their preferences. For someone who cannot easily say, section 4 of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 asks decision makers to consider their past and present wishes and feelings. What families share is one way to know them.

cards.title: A log is not a result
cards.body: Seeing who played a video is useful, but it is a record of plays. It does not tell you how the person felt. The key worker's own observation, written in the home's usual way, still carries the weight.

how.heading: From what the family sent to a better review.

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. The questions are the ones we hear most.

items.q: What can a key worker actually see?
items.a: The From family tab shows what each relative or friend has shared, once a manager has approved it. The Profile tab shows Recently played, which lists who played a video message and when. The key worker still writes the review notes.

items.q: Does CareStream update the dementia care plan?
items.a: No. It does not write to your care records. The key worker or manager records what they have learned in the dementia care plan in your own system. CareStream gives them something to bring to the review.

items.q: Can the log tell us whether a video helped?
items.a: No. It shows who played it and when. It does not record how the person responded, and we do not claim any effect on a condition. What staff observed is for your own notes.

items.q: Can a key worker approve things themselves?
items.a: Approval sits with a manager or admin on the resident's Approvals tab. A key worker can ask for more items to be approved, or for a reminder to be set.

A manager or admin can ask a family contact, by email, to add something new: weekly, fortnightly or monthly. Each email carries a fresh private link and a Stop these reminders link. The default is off.

items.q: Does the chat look at what is in the photos?
items.a: No. Staff find items by the titles, captions and notes people wrote. It never describes a picture or a video, so good titles matter.

items.q: What if the person moves on or passes away?
items.a: Photos and videos leave the hub at once, pending ones are deleted, and reminders stop. Approved files stay in private storage for the retention period, like the written profile, then are deleted with it.

items.q: Which plan is it on, and can I try it?
items.a: Resident profiles, photos and videos are on Professional and above, with a 14 day free trial. See the pricing page. You can create a free account or book a demo.

limits.heading: Honest limits: it shows what was shared and played, nothing more

cards.title: It records plays, not reactions
cards.body: You can see who played a video and when. You cannot see how the person felt, and nothing here shows that it helped. That judgement belongs to the key worker and the team.

cards.title: It is not your care record
cards.body: CareStream does not hold the care plan and does not write to it. What the key worker learns goes into the record your home already uses, and the review stays your process.

cards.title: It cannot see the photos
cards.body: The chat finds items from titles, captions and notes. It does not look inside a picture or a video. The manager's check on the Approvals tab is the safeguard, and relatives cannot see the profile.

faqs.heading: The key worker and the review, answered

items.q: What does a key worker do in a care home?
items.a: Practice varies, and your own policy sets it out. Typically a key worker gets to know one person well, keeps in touch with their family and brings what they learn to reviews. Our guide to the this is me document shows what to record.

items.q: What are good person centred care examples for a review?
items.a: Noting that a choir video is played mid afternoon, asking a daughter for a photo of a place that matters, or adding a favourite song to the plan. Each one is small, specific and tied to the person.

items.q: How should a dementia care plan use what the family shares?
items.a: Record what staff notice and what you plan to do, in your own system. The family's items are a source, and the key worker's observations are the evidence. Review the plan with the person and their family where you can.

items.q: Is the key worker role the same in every care setting?
items.a: No. Some services use different names. The tools on this page work for anyone you ask to review what a family has shared.

Yes. Signed in staff see them through short lived links, and there is no public address. Photos are checked, scanned and saved again without location data, and videos have location and device details removed.
No. They use a private link to add items. They cannot see the profile, and the link is used up when they press Send.

items.q: What does the regulation say about preferences?
items.a: Regulation 9 says care and treatment must be appropriate, meet people's needs and reflect their preferences. Check what this means for your service with your own policies.

items.q: Can I delete an item I approved earlier?
items.a: Yes. You can delete an approved photo or video from the resident's record at any time.

guide.heading: How to prepare a monthly review with what the family shared
guide.lede: A short routine before the review turns scattered comments into something you can act on.

paragraphs: Open the From family tab and look at what is new. Then look at Recently played. Put them next to your own notes from the month. The question is simple: what did we try, and what did we see?
checklist: What has the family shared since the last review?
Which items have staff played, and roughly how often?
What did staff observe, in their own words?
What should the manager approve or ask for next?

paragraphs: Keep observations plain and factual. Write what the person did or said, not what you hope it means. The Mental Capacity Act course helps staff think about wishes and feelings, and the dementia awareness course helps them understand the person behind the diagnosis.

sections.h3: Close the loop with the family
paragraphs: Tell the family what has been used and thank them. If you would like more, ask for something specific, such as a photo of a place or a short clip with a name in the title. A gentle reminder can help, and the family can stop it with one click.

guide.note: This page describes how the software works and is not legal or clinical advice. Check your own policies and local guidance on key worker duties, reviews and care planning.
